dimensions.name: Mechanism and causal judgment
citations: "Their effective_event_date values span 2026-05-01 to 2026-05-28, not just 31 May — sales happened all month; only the posting is clustered"
"It is an expected batch-posting artifact from monthly dealer-file submission"

dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives
citations: "Confidence: Moderate-High (see unknowns below)."
"effective_event_date is dealer-reported and not independently verified against a signed sale record; dates could in theory be adjusted."

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "Do not reverse or hold any of the 17 transactions — the reconciliation already ties out."
"Request the dealer contracts/amendments for DLR-104 and DLR-219 confirming batch-filing terms, and pull the dealer-master region mapping"

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: "## Evidence Table"
"## Unknowns and Decision-Changing Evidence"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "sales happened all month" is stronger than the evidence supports: effective_event_date is dealer-reported and does not independently establish completed sales.

"Pipeline defect (double-ingestion, mis-dated rows) — rejected" is somewhat overconfident. Equal received and accepted counts and recurring cadence address rejects and some ingestion failure modes, but do not rule out a stable systematic date-mapping defect.

"not manipulated reporting" is not fully established by cash-to-ledger reconciliation, because coordinated or upstream manipulation could preserve that reconciliation; the submission partly qualifies this as "on given evidence."

"if the contract can't be produced within a day ... that would flip the judgment toward 'manipulated reporting'" overstates what missing contractual evidence would show; it could establish a policy or compliance issue without demonstrating manipulation.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The strongest alternative is a stable systematic data or source-record issue: dealer-reported effective_event_date values could be wrong or altered even though ingestion is complete, source IDs are unique, and cash reconciles. The submission acknowledges this unknown but does not test it. It also does not explicitly address the important benign-but-material consequence that posting-time clustering can distort downstream retention and trend analytics.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Explicitly recommend that downstream retention and trend analytics use effective_event_date rather than posted_at, while adding a targeted independent validation of effective dates against activation or entitlement records; this would preserve the no-escalation decision while addressing the main remaining risk.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "South-region complaint tickets fell 37% per day after the May 10 pilot start while North, East, and West stayed flat or rose"
"CareDesk only logs a case after a subscriber is authenticated, and 24% of NovaIVR sessions now dead-end at authentication (errors or abandons) before that point, versus 7% in the legacy system."

dimensions.name: Mechanism and causal judgment
citations: "The visible decline is at least partly a change in what gets counted, not proof that self-service resolved more issues."
"Network outage rates in South were unchanged or slightly higher post-pilot, so fewer real problems doesn't explain the drop either."

dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives
citations: "Unknown: whether customers who errored or abandoned at authentication resolved their issue elsewhere, called back through another channel, or simply gave up."
"Unknown: whether any other South-specific change (staffing, IVR menu edits, a campaign) coincided with the May 10 pilot start."

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "Do not expand NovaIVR nationally yet."

"Instrument pre-authentication drop-offs (errors and abandons) as a tracked failure category instead of silence, and re-run the South-vs-other-regions comparison over an equal-length pre/post window before making any national expansion decision."

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: "For the 302 authentication errors (TOKEN_MISMATCH / ANI_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT) in South, is there any way to know if those customers got help elsewhere or went unresolved?"
"Has anyone manually sampled abandoned NovaIVR sessions to check whether the underlying issue was actually fixed?"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "The drop is real and region-specific, not seasonal" is somewhat overstated: flat or rising comparison regions support a South-specific break but do not by themselves rule out all seasonal or calendar effects.

"The case-counting rules changed at the same moment" is directionally supported by the cited policy and pilot timing, but the submission does not provide exact email language or a before/after rule comparison showing that the counting rule itself changed rather than merely becoming relevant for more sessions.

The 302-error figure and the assertion that it represents the relevant South authentication-error population are asked about but not separately traced in the evidence table to a field, cohort, or query.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The submission handled the main benign alternative that fewer genuine network problems caused fewer tickets, and it preserved the possibility that authentication abandoners resolved their issues elsewhere. It did not fully develop the alternative that NovaIVR genuinely improved outcomes for some customers while simultaneously creating a measurement blind spot, nor specify journey-linked evidence that would distinguish those explanations.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Add explicit end-to-end journey linkage for authentication errors and abandons—repeat attempts, alternate-channel contacts, eventual case creation, and a sample of call/session outcomes—while citing the exact source fields and cohort definitions used for each headline metric.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission cites the `timestamp_local` column for the 2026-05-29 08:06 to 2026-06-04 16:18 gap and the `inverter_id` column for the four IDs.
The conclusion cites `low/info severity`, `impact_mw = 0`, and `cleared = yes`, but does not identify the specific file or event rows supporting those fields.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: It considers two plausible explanations for the gap: “a quiet period or a monitoring/logging outage.”

It cross-checks inverter IDs and event outcomes, but the inference that a degrading unit would necessarily recur is not sufficiently tested; four unique IDs alone do not rule out a unit-specific or broader issue.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: The analyst explicitly says the gap “can't tell from this file alone” and labels confidence medium.
The proposed heartbeat/uptime check is a small, decision-changing request rather than a broad request for more investigation.

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: “No basis to escalate” follows from zero MW impact, cleared events, and low/info severity.
The recommendation to confirm monitoring continuity from 2026-05-29 through 2026-06-04 is proportionate and discriminates between a real quiet period and missing telemetry.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: The conclusion avoids inventing a plant problem from the available event records and appropriately recommends stopping after a cheap monitoring-integrity check.
It is consistent with the supplied event facts: zero impact, quick/cleared events, and no repeated inverter ID.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: “No pattern of a single unit recurring” is directly observed, but “so no unit-specific degradation pattern” is overstated: non-repetition across four events does not exclude degradation or a problem that has not yet recurred.
“A failing unit would typically show repeated events on the same ID” is a plausible heuristic, not evidence established by the supplied records.

The statement that all events are low/info severity, have zero MW impact, and are cleared is not fully traceable to named rows or a file in the evidence table, although it is consistent with the submission’s cited event fields.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The six-day interval may simply be a normal quiet period rather than a logging outage, and the unique inverter IDs may reflect unrelated transient events rather than evidence against degradation. The proposed heartbeat/uptime check is the right way to distinguish the timing interpretations without escalating on speculation.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Make the operational conclusion traceable to the individual event rows, including each event’s severity, impact_mw, cleared status, and any communication-warning wording; retain the heartbeat/uptime check as the only follow-up if those rows confirm zero impact and rapid recovery.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission identifies specific sources and fields: “dispatch_blocks.csv (recomputed),” “schedule_source column,” and the “13:00-15:45” block range.

It distinguishes the observed 31.6% result from the broader causal claim, but does not show the underlying block values, calculation, or quantify the same-day base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw counterfactual.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: It uses multiple channels, including dispatch blocks, schedule-source tags, the commercial extract, and additional stow days.
It identifies an important mechanism and limitation: “whether the benefit requires the AI/forecast component specifically, versus any timely rule-based schedule cut.”

The claim that weather variability is “rejected” because the days had “similar gust ranges” is too strong; matching duration and broadly similar gusts do not eliminate other day-specific weather or operational differences.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: The submission explicitly narrows the conclusion: “This is not yet evidence that ‘AI-assisted scheduling’ causes a systematic ~30% DSM reduction.”
It labels the general-causation claim low confidence, identifies the missing intervention on 28 May, and proposes 8-10 additional events plus a rule-based comparison arm.
It also acknowledges the imperfect comparison of 3 and 4 June because “stow durations differ.”

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: The recommendation to continue in “parallel/shadow-run mode rather than as the sole operational schedule” is proportionate to the causal uncertainty.
The proposed parallel non-AI rule-based arm is a discriminating next test rather than generic data collection.
Monitoring the “post-stow recovery ramp” is linked to the observed result that “2 of the 12 revised blocks” underperformed the base schedule.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: The submission correctly rejects generalizing the 31.6% interday result into a systematic causal effect and retains a positive, narrower interpretation rather than concluding there is no value.

However, “lowering the submitted schedule ... reduced DSM exposure” remains somewhat causal and the submission does not explicitly report the smaller same-day benefit from the 29 May base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw comparison, which is the key qualification.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: “Rejected: ‘the gap is purely weather variability’” is overstated: similar stow duration and gust ranges make weather variability less compelling but do not reject it as a contributor.

“The gain traces to ... reducing the deviation band” is a plausible mechanism, but the submission does not show the block-level base_schedule_mw, submitted_schedule_mw, actual output, or DSM calculations needed to establish that mechanism quantitatively.

“On this one matched day-pair ... lowering the submitted schedule ... reduced DSM exposure” should be framed as an observed same-day counterfactual association unless the same-day recalculation is explicitly shown.
The claim that the 31.6% figures “reproduce exactly” is not independently demonstrated in the submission because the numerical recomputation is not displayed.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The 31.6% headline may primarily reflect differences between 28 and 29 May rather than the intervention. The 29 May same-day base-versus-submitted schedule comparison can support a smaller positive operational effect, but remaining weather, forecast, dispatch, and recovery-ramp differences prevent attributing the full interday reduction to AI-assisted scheduling.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Explicitly calculate and report the 29 May same-day counterfactual for every affected block using base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw, including the resulting aggregate DSM difference and the recovery-ramp penalty. This would separate the smaller intervention-associated benefit from the 31.6% between-day comparison.

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: "Do not escalate as a declaration error."
"Fix the automated check to compare CH declarations against the Swiss Matrix (not Helios)"
"separately confirm 90211000 against Tares or the broker"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "Switzerland's own approved local classification" is stronger than the stated source limitation that the Swiss Matrix is only an internal working reference, not a verified legal ruling.
The claim that "the automated flag compared it against" Helios is not tied to a cited flag rule, event, or comparison log.
"global/EU-oriented" and "cross-jurisdiction string matches aren't expected" describe system design but are not directly evidenced by a cited configuration or documentation passage.
"Genuine misclassification: rejected" is somewhat too categorical because no official Tares result or product-specific ruling was checked.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The alert is most likely a benign Swiss-versus-Helios code-system mismatch, but the Swiss code could still be legally incorrect or the detector could be using an undocumented comparison rule; the available evidence establishes internal consistency, not definitive regulatory correctness.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Cite the exact Swiss Matrix row and detector/configuration or alert-comparison record, then verify 90211000 in the official Tares database before making the non-escalation and rule-change decisions.

"The specific trade rule/agreement the broker used to justify 'Preference: Yes.'"

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: "Do not treat the claim as confirmed."
"Request an up-to-date supplier declaration from Procurement Shared Services before relying on the preference"
"flag the line for review rather than amending or cancelling unilaterally"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "Declared origin = US, Preference = Yes" is described as "internally inconsistent with a preference claim," but US manufacturing and US preferential origin are not inherently inconsistent; the applicable agreement and origin rule are needed to assess validity.
The evidence table identifies sources but does not provide exact file identifiers, row numbers, document excerpts, or the relevant preference rule, limiting independent verification.
A document expired on 2025-07-31 does not by itself establish that the shipment dated 2025-09-18 lacked valid supplier evidence; it supports a documentation gap, not invalidity.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The preference claim may still be valid if SUP-01 or SUP-02 supplied the batch under an applicable agreement and can substantiate the required originating status through a current declaration or production records; the stale register may reflect administrative lag rather than a substantive origin failure.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Trace the actual supplier and applicable trade rule for P1006, then cite the specific supplier declaration or production evidence and explain whether it satisfies that rule for the 2025-09-18 shipment.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "84% (185/220) of qcore_release_ts times are exactly 02:10:00" — precise field, count, and source citation support the central anomaly.

"42/262 rows are open HOLD" and "30 of those HOLDs are over 24h past evidence-ready" — relevant cross-file claims are cited, but the submission does not provide row-level identifiers or reconcile the later reference to "30 MISSING/INDEX_PENDING RELEASED batches."
"coa_status gap likely a CertVault index-lag artifact" — source freshness is relevant, but the causal interpretation is only indirectly evidenced.

dimensions.name: Causal / investigative reasoning
citations: "consistent with QCore's daily batch refresh ... rather than a live disposition clock" — distinguishes a measurement/interface mechanism from the apparent cycle-time symptom.

"an 84% clustering at one exact clock-time is not random variance, it's a system artifact" — correctly identifies a strong timing anomaly, but exact clustering does not by itself distinguish extract stamping from a genuinely scheduled release process.
"ask QCore/IT for the true authorization-event timestamp ... versus the extract's write timestamp" — proposes a discriminating test rather than treating the mechanism as proven.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: "Do not publish '~1.5 days' ... yet" and the use of "consistent with" and "likely" — appropriately withholds KPI use while preserving hypotheses.

The table labels several claims "High" confidence, including "QCore refreshes only daily, not live" and the HOLD interpretation; these labels overstate what extract freshness alone establishes and do not explicitly address that QCore/LabTrack extracts may not be a coherent snapshot.
"Medium" confidence for the CertVault explanation acknowledges uncertainty, though the submission still treats that explanation as the primary one without direct event evidence.

dimensions.name: Decision usefulness / reframing
citations: "Do not publish '~1.5 days' as a release-cycle KPI yet" — directly reframes the decision from optimizing a potentially invalid metric to validating timestamp semantics.
"require any KPI to separately report open-HOLD backlog age" — protects against hiding in-progress work while preserving a useful operational measure.
"ask QCore/IT for the true authorization-event timestamp ... and require ... backlog age" — small, reversible actions that create evidence and reduce reporting risk.

dimensions.name: Disconfirmation and rejected hypotheses
citations: The submission rejects normal variance using the 02:10 concentration, rejects treating HOLD work as irrelevant, and tests a stale-index alternative for CertVault.

"more likely a stale read than a true gap" is plausible but not established; the strongest competing explanation—that QCore uses a scheduled but semantically valid release process—should have been stated explicitly and tested with event/audit records.
"What Would Change the Decision" identifies evidence that could revive the competing timestamp interpretation.

dimensions.name: Questioning / next evidence
citations: "ask QCore/IT for the true authorization-event timestamp (audit log) versus the extract's write timestamp" — high-value, narrowly scoped query that directly discriminates workflow delay from interface timing.

"A live pull (not the nightly CertVault index)" and confirmation from the Site/Quality lead on overdue HOLD exception coding — targeted follow-ups tied to separate decisions rather than a generic request for more data.
The requested audit/event evidence would determine whether the KPI can be defined and published, while the backlog and CertVault checks address operational and data-quality consequences.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "QCore refreshes only daily, not live" and the statement that elapsed-time math is "quantized to roughly 24h" conflate extract refresh timing with the semantics of the underlying release event; the evidence supports a serious timestamp concern, not yet that the release process itself is daily or quantized.
The CertVault explanation that the coa_status gap is "likely ... an index-lag artifact" is reasonable but not demonstrated by the cited freshness row alone.
The submission inconsistently refers first to 30 overdue HOLDs and later to "30 MISSING/INDEX_PENDING RELEASED batches"; those populations should be reconciled before acting on the claim.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The 02:10 concentration could reflect a scheduled, valid QCore authorization or release process rather than merely an extract-write artifact. In that case the metric may still be operationally meaningful, but it would measure scheduled/interface release timing rather than the decision time defined by the SOP. An audit/event log linking required-evidence availability, authorization, and extract commit would distinguish these interpretations.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Obtain and reconcile a small event-level sample containing required-evidence-available time, authorization/decision time, QCore extract-write time, and source snapshot timestamps; use it to define the KPI before interpreting the 1.5-day value or attributing overdue HOLDs and certificate gaps.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "RI-0001 and ME-0003 servo drives show available_qty_global equal to on-hand, but are flagged reserved_for_critical_asset=true" — cites spare_parts.csv and part_restrictions.csv with relevant fields.
"Inventory snapshot (MaintStar-global) is ~5 weeks older than the restrictions snapshot" — cites source_freshness.csv.
"Northport/Meridian requests duplicate parts already on their own shelves under different descriptions" — identifies the request and inventory sources and gives an example.

dimensions.name: Causal / investigative reasoning
citations: "available_qty_global can be trusted at face value" — rejected using negative quantities and the maintenance email's reservation warning.
"Any description-level match is interchangeable" — rejected because VLV-3722 rev A and rev B are not shown to be equivalent.
"The problem is purely cross-site" — rejected by identifying same-site duplicate purchasing as an alternative mechanism.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: "Needs check" for VLV-3722, BLT-7302, and revision substitution, rather than treating semantic matches as transfers.
"High for staleness, Low for 'stock levels are current'" — explicitly distinguishes freshness evidence from current availability.
"~15% ... is defensibly actionable now" is qualified by the stale snapshot but still presents a precise aggregate that is not fully auditable from the submission.

dimensions.name: Decision usefulness / reframing
citations: "The biggest real win isn't cross-site transfer at all" — usefully reframes the opportunity toward same-site duplicate prevention.
The table separates "Actionable now / Needs check / Not transferable" and identifies reservation, revision, supply-demand, and reconciliation safeguards.
The submission does not define a small reversible pilot, approval workflow, or success criteria before acting on the 'actionable now' matches.

dimensions.name: Disconfirmation and rejected hypotheses
citations: "All reserved-critical stock is permanently off-limits" — not assumed; the analyst requests a re-check.
"Any description-level match is interchangeable" and "available_qty_global can be trusted at face value" are explicitly rejected with case-specific evidence.
The submission does not fully test alternative explanations for same-site duplicate requests, such as intentional local stocking, UOM differences, or qualification constraints.

dimensions.name: Questioning / next evidence
citations: Requests a "live (not monthly) stock pull" to resolve stale and negative availability.
Requests engineering sign-off on VLV-3722 revision substitution and confirmation of current servo-drive reservations.
The requests are highly relevant and decision-linked, but are listed together rather than prioritized by expected value or tied to explicit decision thresholds.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The exact aggregate conclusion — "only ~15% ($23.6k) is defensibly actionable now," with 31% needing checks and 54% not transferable — is not accompanied by a line-level reconciliation showing how every request, quantity, price, UOM, and restriction was classified.

Calling the listed PMP-2288, SNS-9910, BRG-1507, FLT-1199, and PLC-8840 matches "Actionable now" may overstate certainty because the submission does not show qualification, UOM, current reservation, or other transferability checks for each candidate, and the MaintStar inventory snapshot is stale.
"The biggest real win" from same-site duplicate purchasing is plausible but not demonstrated with an aggregate value comparison against cross-site opportunities.

The conclusion that the servo-drive issue is "the same false-positive pattern" is reasonable from the email and restriction flags, but one prior declined transfer does not establish a general pattern without broader historical evidence.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: Some apparent same-site duplicate purchases may be intentional rather than search failures—for example, the request and shelf item could differ in UOM, qualification, revision, lifecycle status, or local operational policy. Likewise, the stale inventory and restriction extracts may be temporally inconsistent enough that the clean-looking matches are candidate opportunities rather than actionable transfers.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Produce a line-level decision ledger for every request-to-stock match that joins manufacturer part number, revision, UOM, qualification, quantity, reservation/criticality, site, price, and source timestamp; then validate the highest-value candidates with a live MaintStar pull and engineering/maintenance approval. This would test the 15% actionable estimate and prevent stale or non-equivalent stock from being treated as avoided purchases.
